name: Evermere Senior Living
tagline: A home on the water, built around the people in it.
description: Evermere is a residential senior living community on the shore of a quiet lake in the Puget Sound region of Washington. headline: Morning light on the lake, and the rest of the day is yours.
intro: Evermere is a residential senior living community on a quiet Washington shoreline. Private suites, warm shared rooms and a team who knows your name, in a home designed for the life you still want to live.

chapters.heading: There is a moment, coming up the drive, when the lake appears.
body: The road bends through a stand of Douglas fir, the trees open, and the water is there: still, silver in the morning, gold by evening. Most people who visit Evermere remember that moment first.
We built the home around it. Every shared room faces the courtyard or the lake, and most suites see one or the other.

image.alt: A still lake under morning mist, with dark evergreens reflected along the far shore.
image.usage: Home opening hero; first frame of the journey

chapters.heading: A home first, and a community because of it.
body: Evermere is a residence for older adults who want their own space, their own routines and the ease of good company close by. It is not a hospital and it does not look like one. It is a place to live.

Residents keep their furniture, their mornings and their opinions. What changes is the work they no longer have to do alone: the cooking, the upkeep, the long winter evenings, the worry of a family three hours away.

image.alt: Tall pines on a point of land at dawn, with mist lifting off calm water.

chapters.heading: Cedar, glass and a long view of the water.
body: The residence is a two-story Northwest contemporary building in cedar and glass, with deep eaves that keep the rain off a covered porch running the length of the lakeside.
A level path follows the shore past benches and a small dock. Behind the house, the trees hold the quiet in.

image.alt: A two-story contemporary residence of timber, dark stone and glass among tall pines, with a stone path across the lawn to the entrance.
image.usage: Home arrival and surroundings; Our home opening

chapters.heading: Come in. The fire is already lit.
body: The front door opens into the Commons: a tall living room with a stone fireplace, deep chairs and windows onto the courtyard. It is where people meet before lunch, read the paper and wave to visitors.
There is no front desk to check in at. Someone will simply say hello.

image.alt: A covered entrance clad in warm cedar boards beside a stone column, with plants in the foreground.

chapters.heading: Rooms for being alone, and rooms for being together.
body: Private suites are quiet, light and yours to furnish. Each has its own bathroom, generous closets and windows that open.
A few steps away are the Library, the Garden Room, the Studio and the Dining Room. Some days you will want all of them. Some days you will want your own door and a good book. Both are right.

image.alt: A light-filled suite with pale wood floors, a reading chair, a bed and a wall of windows.

chapters.heading: The shape of the day is up to you.
body: Coffee on the porch, a walk along the shore, a watercolor class in the Studio, an afternoon nap, a card game that runs long. The calendar is full, and none of it is required.
Residents help shape what happens here, from the book club reading list to the next trip into town.

image.alt: A person paints in watercolor at a sunny window beside a vase of lilies.

chapters.heading: A long table, a seasonal menu and time to talk.
body: Meals are cooked in our own kitchen with Washington produce, seafood and orchard fruit when the season allows. The Dining Room looks across the courtyard, and conversation tends to outlast dessert.
Prefer breakfast in your suite or a later lunch? Tell the kitchen. Family is always welcome at the table.

image.alt: A dining room with a long wooden table beneath a pendant light and windows onto bare winter trees.

chapters.heading: Support that fits around your life, not the other way around.
body: Everyone at Evermere has a personal plan, written together with the resident and, when they wish, their family. It describes the help someone wants, the routines that matter to them and the things they would rather keep doing themselves.
The plan changes when life does. Our team is here day and night, and we explain exactly what support is available during your first conversation with us.

image.alt: An older couple walk away along a tree-lined path by the water, arm in arm.

chapters.heading: Weather is not a reason to stay inside.
body: The courtyard garden has raised planting beds at standing and seated heights, a covered walk and a fire table for cool evenings. In summer, the dock is the best seat in the house.
Paths are level, lit and edged for steady walking, and there is always a bench within sight.

image.alt: A covered walkway under a warm timber ceiling, open on one side to a planted gravel garden with boulders.

chapters.heading: Families are part of the household.
body: Children and grandchildren visit when they like, stay for dinner, bring the dog and join the summer picnic. A guest suite can be reserved for family traveling from farther away.
We keep families informed in the way each resident prefers, and we welcome their questions at any hour.

image.alt: A grandfather and grandmother look at photographs with their granddaughter at the table.

chapters.heading: See it for yourself, in every season.
body: Photographs can show you the light, the rooms and the view. They cannot show you how it feels to sit by the fire on a wet November afternoon. For that, you will have to visit.

image.alt: A shaded path through pines along the lakeshore, with two benches facing the water.

chapters.heading: Come for coffee. Stay as long as you like.
body: The best way to understand Evermere is to spend an hour here. Walk the halls, see a suite, have lunch with us and ask every question you have. There is no obligation, and nothing to sign.

image.alt: Two dark Adirondack chairs on a wet dock facing a calm lake and forested hills.

title: About Evermere
headline: We started with a simple question: where would we want to live?
intro: Evermere was imagined as the kind of place its founders would choose for their own parents, and one day for themselves. Small enough to know everyone, comfortable enough to feel like home, and respectful of the fact that the people who live here have spent a lifetime making their own decisions.

sections.heading: What we believe
body: Growing older does not make anyone less themselves. Our residents arrive with careers, families, convictions, favorite chairs and strong views on how coffee should be made. A good home makes room for all of it.
So we try to do the opposite of an institution. We learn how each person likes to live, then shape our help around that, rather than asking people to fit a schedule written for someone else.

image.alt: A woman with short gray hair listens to a friend over coffee among tall plants.

sections.heading: The name
body: A mere is an old English word for a lake. Evermere is a promise about this particular place: the water will be here every morning, and so will we.

sections.heading: How we work
body: These principles guide decisions large and small, from how we design a suite to how we answer the phone.
points: Choice comes first. Residents decide how they spend their days, and we ask before we assume.
Independence is something to protect. We help with what someone wants help with and step back from the rest.
Belonging is built in small moments: a name remembered, a seat saved, a birthday noticed.
Families are partners. We listen to them, keep them informed in the way each resident prefers and welcome them at any time.
We are honest, especially when the answer is complicated.

sections.heading: A residence, not a campus
body: Evermere is one home on one shoreline. There are no towers, no long corridors with numbered doors and no parking lots between you and the water. The building is low, warm and easy to find your way around.

image.alt: The same residence seen between pine trunks, with stepping stones leading to glass doors.

sections.heading: The people who make it work
body: A home is only as good as the people looking after it. Our team includes resident support, culinary, life enrichment, housekeeping and maintenance staff, and everyone is expected to know residents by name.

image.alt: An older couple walk away along a tree-lined path by the water, arm in arm.

title: Our home
headline: A Northwest house, built around a garden and facing the water.
intro: Evermere sits on a gentle rise above a quiet lake, ringed by Douglas fir and western red cedar. The building borrows from the region's own architecture: low rooflines, deep eaves, honest materials and big windows that bring the weather in without letting it reach you.

sections.heading: Cedar, stone and a great deal of glass
body: The residence is two stories of cedar, dark stone and glass, arranged in a U around a sheltered courtyard. The open side of the U faces the lake, so the garden and the water are visible from almost every shared room.

Inside, there is warm oak underfoot, plaster walls in soft neutral tones and ceilings that rise where people gather. Corridors are short and full of daylight, with windows at each turn so it is always easy to know where you are.

image.alt: A two-story house of cedar boards and dark stone panels among pines, with long windows facing a sunlit lawn.

sections.heading: The Commons
body: Just inside the front door, the Commons is the living room of the house. A stone fireplace anchors one end, a grand piano the other, and the long wall of windows looks onto the courtyard. It is the natural place to meet a friend, wait for a ride or simply sit somewhere with people nearby.

image.alt: A bright living room with a stacked-stone fireplace and tall windows looking into the trees.

sections.heading: Rooms with a purpose
body: Around the Commons are smaller rooms, each made for something specific.
points: The Library: quiet, carpeted and lined with shelves, with reading chairs by the window and a table for puzzles that take a week.
The Garden Room: a glass-walled sunroom for plants, morning coffee and afternoons when the sun finally comes out.
The Studio: a bright workroom with sinks, easels and long tables for painting, clay, flower arranging and repair projects.
The Dining Room: a high-ceilinged room with views across the courtyard, set with tables for two, four and more.
The Lake Room: a flexible space for exercise classes, lectures, films and family celebrations.

image.alt: A library with floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, wing chairs beside a tiled fireplace and tall windows onto evergreens.

sections.heading: The courtyard
body: The heart of Evermere is outdoors. The courtyard garden has raised beds at standing and seated heights, a covered walkway on three sides and a fire table for the cool Northwest evenings. It is fully enclosed, level and planted to look good in every season, from spring tulips to winter grasses.

image.alt: A covered walkway under a warm timber ceiling, open on one side to a planted gravel garden with boulders.

sections.heading: The shore
body: A level, lit path leads from the porch to the water and follows the shoreline past benches and a small dock. Herons work the shallows in the morning. In summer, residents fish, sketch, read and watch the light change on the far bank.

image.alt: A shaded path through pines along the lakeshore, with two benches facing the water.

sections.heading: Designed for ease, without looking like it
body: Doorways are wide, floors are level and handrails are built into the woodwork rather than bolted on. Lighting is warm and even, with no harsh glare. These details make the house easier to live in for everyone, and most visitors never notice them.

image.alt: Horizontal cedar slats stepping out against a clear blue sky.

title: Accommodations
headline: Your own front door, your own furniture, your own view.
intro: Every Evermere suite is a private home within the larger house. Bring the furniture you love, hang your own pictures and close the door when you want to. We provide the light, the space and the upkeep.

sections.heading: Three kinds of suite
body: Suites come in three layouts, so you can choose the amount of space that suits the way you live. Exact sizes, layouts and current availability are shared during a personal conversation, because they vary from suite to suite.

sections.heading: In every suite
body: Each suite is designed to feel residential rather than clinical, with practical features that make daily life easier.
points: A private bathroom with a walk-in shower, seat and slip-resistant floor.
Windows that open, with views of the courtyard or the lake.
Generous closets and built-in storage.
Individual heating and cooling controls.
A kitchenette with a small refrigerator and space for a kettle.
Telephone, cable and internet connections.
Weekly housekeeping and linen service.

image.alt: A suite bedroom with an upholstered bed, bedside lamps and a door open to a private bathroom.

sections.heading: Make it yours
body: The most important furniture in any suite is the furniture you bring. We will help you plan what fits before moving day, and our maintenance team will hang pictures, mount shelves and set up lamps so everything is where you want it.
If you would prefer not to bring everything, we can furnish a suite with simple pieces that you can replace over time.

cta.label: Read: helping a loved one feel at home

image.alt: A walnut dresser and a tall mirror reflecting the bed, beside a window onto the woods.

sections.heading: For couples
body: Couples can share a larger suite together. If partners need different levels of support, we will talk honestly about what is possible so they can stay close.

image.alt: A woman and a man play cards at a round wooden table in a bright room.

sections.heading: A room for family
body: Evermere has a guest suite that families can reserve when they visit from out of town, so a long journey can end with a good night's sleep down the hall.

title: Care and support
headline: Help with the parts of the day you choose, and respect for the rest.
intro: Support at Evermere begins with a conversation, not a checklist. We want to understand how someone likes to live, what they enjoy doing for themselves and where a little help would make life easier. Then we write a personal plan together and keep it current.

sections.heading: Our approach
body: Good support is mostly invisible. It looks like a morning that starts at the right time, a favorite sweater that is clean when it is wanted and a friendly check-in that does not feel like an inspection.
We pay attention to the details that make someone feel like themselves, and we step back from anything a resident would rather manage alone.

image.alt: A woman with short gray hair listens to a friend over coffee among tall plants.

sections.heading: A personal plan, written together
body: Before moving in, each resident meets with our team to talk through routines, preferences and any help they would like. With the resident's permission, family members are welcome to join. The result is a written plan that every team member follows.
Plans are reviewed regularly and whenever something changes. Nobody's support is decided without them.

image.alt: An older woman in a white robe reads in a wingback chair.

sections.heading: How we can help
body: The support available at Evermere is described below in general terms. The specific services offered, and how they are provided, are explained in full during a personal consultation so that every family has accurate information for their situation.

sections.heading: Working with your own providers
body: Many residents keep their own physicians, therapists and specialists. We help with scheduling and transportation to appointments, and with the resident's permission we stay in touch with the people involved in their health.

image.alt: Three women stretch on yoga mats in a bright studio with shelves of equipment.
image.usage: Lifestyle movement; Care and support wellbeing

sections.heading: Straight answers
body: Every person's needs are different, and they can change over time. If a question cannot be answered on a web page, we would rather talk it through with you properly. Call us, write to us or ask during a visit.

title: Lifestyle
headline: A full calendar, and the freedom to ignore it.
intro: Life at Evermere is as social or as private as each resident wants it to be. There is always something happening, from morning stretch class to an evening concert in the Commons, and there is never any pressure to join in.

sections.heading: The rhythm of a day
body: Mornings start slowly, with coffee in the Garden Room and the newspaper by the fire. Late morning is for classes, walks and appointments. After lunch, the house quiets for an hour before the afternoon brings clubs, workshops and visitors. Evenings belong to dinner, conversation and whatever is on in the Lake Room.
That is the general shape. The details belong to the residents.

image.alt: A woman sips coffee in an armchair by a window with plants on the sill.

sections.heading: Keep doing what you love
body: Our life enrichment coordinator builds the calendar with residents, not for them. If enough people want a watercolor group, a Spanish conversation table or a woodworking project, we make room for it.
points: Art and making: painting, clay, flower arranging and small repair projects in the Studio.
Mind: book club, lectures, current-events discussion and a language table.
Movement: stretching, chair yoga, walking groups along the shore and gentle strength classes.
Music: live performances in the Commons, sing-alongs and listening sessions.
Garden: seasonal planting in the courtyard beds and a cutting garden for the dining tables.

image.alt: A woman with long gray braids harvests lettuce from a raised vegetable bed.

sections.heading: Beyond the front door
body: Evermere's own vehicle takes residents into town for shopping, appointments, concerts and lunches out. Seasonal trips visit gardens, ferries, farm stands and museums around the Sound.

image.alt: An older couple walk together on a lakeside path between birch trees.

sections.heading: A chance to contribute
body: Many residents spent decades teaching, building, nursing, managing and raising families. They have a great deal to offer. Residents lead clubs, teach classes, welcome new neighbors and help plan events, and their ideas shape the calendar.

image.alt: Three women play cards around a small table with glasses of juice.

sections.heading: And room for quiet
body: Not everyone wants a busy day, and that is fine. A good book in a sunny window, a nap after lunch or a long phone call with a grandchild are all part of life here, too.

image.alt: A woman reads in a wooden armchair beside a sunny window lined with plants.

title: Amenities
headline: Everything close by, so the day is easier to enjoy.
intro: The practical comforts at Evermere are designed to remove small burdens and leave more time for the things that matter. Most are included in daily life here; a personal conversation is the best way to learn exactly what is included for each suite.

sections.heading: Around the house
body: Shared rooms are open throughout the day and evening, and residents are welcome to use them with their guests.
points: The Commons, with fireplace and grand piano.
The Library, with large-print books, audiobooks and a puzzle table.
The Garden Room, a sunroom for plants and morning coffee.
The Studio, for art and craft projects.
The Lake Room, for classes, films and private family events.
A salon for hair appointments and nail care.
A private dining room for family celebrations.

image.alt: A bright sitting room with a pale sofa, woven chairs and a row of high windows onto pine trees.

sections.heading: Outdoors
body: The grounds are level, lit and designed for steady walking in all seasons.
points: An enclosed courtyard garden with raised planting beds.
A covered walkway and fire table.
A lakeside path with benches and a small dock.
A covered porch along the lake side of the house.

title: Dining
headline: Good food, cooked here, and a table worth lingering at.
intro: Meals are one of the great pleasures of a day, and we treat them that way. Our kitchen cooks from scratch, follows the Washington seasons and serves residents in a dining room with a view across the courtyard.

sections.heading: From our own kitchen
body: The culinary team writes menus around what is good right now: spring asparagus, summer berries, Pacific salmon, autumn apples from the orchards east of the mountains. Familiar favorites stay on the menu all year, because some days only a good soup and a grilled cheese sandwich will do.

image.alt: A crusted salmon fillet on whipped potatoes with lemon and herbs in a handmade ceramic bowl.

sections.heading: Through the day
body: Breakfast is relaxed and served over a long morning. Lunch is the social meal of the day. Dinner is calmer, with candles on the tables in winter and the doors open to the courtyard in summer. Coffee, tea, fruit and snacks are available between meals.

image.alt: A cup of coffee on a wooden table in low morning sunlight.

sections.heading: Your table, your way
body: Residents choose where and when to eat. Join friends at a large table, sit with one companion by the window, or take breakfast in your suite on a slow morning.
The kitchen accommodates dietary preferences and needs, and the chef is happy to talk through them personally.

image.alt: Croissants, butter and mugs of coffee on a sunlit breakfast table.

sections.heading: Meals with family
body: Families and friends are always welcome to join for a meal. The private dining room can be reserved for birthdays, anniversaries and holiday gatherings, with a menu planned together with the chef.

image.alt: An older couple raise glasses of red wine across a table by a window.

sections.heading: Celebrating the year
body: The calendar is marked by food: a summer picnic on the lawn, a harvest dinner, holiday baking in the Studio and a crab feed when the season allows. These are some of the most popular days of the year.

image.alt: A summer salad of tomatoes, shaved cucumber and herbs on a white plate, seen from above.

title: Our team
headline: The people who know your name, and how you take your coffee.
intro: The Evermere team is small by design. Staff work in consistent roles with the same residents over time, so relationships can grow and nothing important has to be explained twice.

sections.heading: Who does what
body: Each part of the team has a clear role, and everyone shares the same responsibility: to treat Evermere as the residents' home and to act like guests in it.

sections.heading: How we choose people
body: We hire for warmth, judgment and reliability, then train for everything else. Every team member is introduced to residents personally and learns each person's plan and preferences before working with them.

sections.heading: A direct line for families
body: Families can always reach a member of our team. We agree with each resident how and when their family will be updated, and we follow that agreement carefully.

title: Contact
headline: Let's talk, whenever you are ready.
intro: Whether you are starting to research, comparing communities or ready to visit, we are glad to help. Call, write or send a message below, and a member of our team will reply within one business day.

sections.heading: What happens next
body: There is no pressure and no obligation at any stage. Most families follow a path like this one.
points: A first conversation by phone or email, to understand who you are asking for and what matters most.

title: Privacy notice
headline: Privacy notice
intro: This notice explains what information Evermere collects through this website, why we collect it and how it is handled. It is a demonstration notice and will be reviewed before the site is published.

sections.heading: Information we collect
body: The inquiry form asks for your name and email address and, if you choose, a telephone number, a topic, how you prefer to be contacted and a short message. Please do not share medical, insurance or financial information through the website.
Like most websites, our servers may record basic technical information, such as browser type and the pages requested, to keep the site secure and working.

sections.heading: How we use it
body: We use inquiry details only to respond to you, to arrange visits you request and to follow up on your questions. We do not sell personal information, and we do not use it for unrelated marketing.

sections.heading: Who we share it with
body: During this preview, the inquiry form is a demonstration: the website checks each message for completeness and then discards it, so nothing is sent or stored. When it goes live, inquiries will be delivered to our team through a secure email service. We will share information with service providers only as needed to operate the website and respond to you, or where the law requires it.

sections.heading: Your choices
body: You may ask us what information we hold about you, ask us to correct it or ask us to delete it. Contact us at privacy@example.com or (206) 555-0142.

sections.heading: Changes to this notice
body: We will update this notice if our practices change and will show the date of the latest revision on this page.

title: Accessibility
headline: Accessibility
intro: We want everyone to be able to use this website comfortably, including people who use screen readers, keyboard navigation, magnification or captions.

sections.heading: Our goal
body: This website is designed to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. We test with automated tools and keyboard navigation, screen-reader testing is under way, and we review new content before it is published.

sections.heading: What we have done
points: Text and interface colors meet recommended contrast levels.
Every page can be used with a keyboard, with a clearly visible focus indicator.
Images have text descriptions.
Motion is reduced or removed when your device asks for reduced motion.
Text can be enlarged without loss of content.

sections.heading: Tell us if something is not working

title: What to look for when choosing a senior living community
summary: A practical way to compare communities, beyond the brochure: the questions that reveal how a place really works.

image.alt: The same residence seen between pine trunks, with stepping stones leading to glass doors.

children.text: Most senior living communities look good in photographs. The differences that matter, such as how people are treated, how decisions are made and what daily life actually feels like, are harder to see. This guide offers a practical way to look past the brochure, whether you are choosing for yourself or helping someone you love.
Start with the person, not the building

Before you visit anywhere, spend some time on what a good day looks like for the person who will live there. Do they rise early or late? Do they want a busy social calendar or a few close friends? Is a garden important, or a library, or being near family? Write down three or four things that would make a place feel like home, and three or four that would make it feel wrong. This short list will keep you focused when every community starts to sound the same.

It is also worth being honest about the kind of help that is needed now, and what might be needed later. You do not need to have every answer, but having a rough picture will help you ask better questions.
Watch how people treat each other

The single most revealing thing about a community is the way staff and residents interact when nobody is performing. During a visit, notice whether team members greet residents by name, knock before entering a room and speak to older adults as adults. Notice whether residents talk easily with each other. A warm, ordinary exchange in a hallway tells you more than any tour.
Do staff seem unhurried, or stretched?
Are residents offered choices, or simply told what happens next?
Does the atmosphere feel like a home, an office or a hospital?
Ask how daily life is decided

Every community publishes an activity calendar. Ask who writes it, how often it changes and what happens if a resident wants something that is not on it. Ask whether people can choose when to get up, when to eat and where to spend their time. The answers will tell you how much a community values independence in practice, not just on paper.
Understand the support, clearly

Support services and how they are provided vary widely between communities, and in Washington they are governed by state rules that depend on the type of community. Ask each community to explain, in plain language, what help is available, who provides it and how it is planned with each resident. Ask how plans are reviewed and what happens when someone's needs change. If something is unclear, ask for it in writing.

For questions about licensing, a community's regulatory history or a specific health situation, rely on official state resources and the advice of the person's own physician rather than marketing materials.
Look at the practical details

Small details shape daily life. Check how far it is from a suite to the dining room, whether windows open, how loud the corridors are and whether outdoor spaces are easy to reach and safe to walk. Look at the bathrooms. Ask what can be brought from home, and whether furniture can be moved and pictures hung.
Talk about costs early

Ask what is included in a monthly fee and what is charged separately, how and when fees change, and what deposits or agreements are involved. A good community will explain this patiently and put it in writing. Comparing costs is much easier when you ask each community the same questions. Before signing anything, many families find it helpful to review agreements with a trusted adviser.
Trust what you see more than what you hear

Visit more than once, ideally at different times of day. Stay for a meal. If possible, talk with residents and their families. Then give yourself time to reflect. The right community is usually the one where the person who will live there can picture themselves on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon.

title: Preparing for a visit to a senior living community
summary: How to plan a visit that shows you what you need to know, with questions to bring and things to notice while you are there.

image.alt: Double wooden front doors stand open from a hallway onto a covered porch and tall pines.
image.usage: Contact visiting; Through the Door motif

children.text: A visit is the best way to understand a senior living community, but a single guided tour can blur into the next one. A little preparation makes each visit more useful, and makes it far easier to compare communities afterward.
Decide who should come

If you are visiting on behalf of a parent or partner, bring them if you possibly can. Their reactions matter more than anyone's, and they will notice things you will not. If several family members are involved in the decision, try to visit together, or plan for each to visit once so that nobody is deciding from a description.
Choose the time thoughtfully

Ask to visit when the community is ordinary rather than staged: mid-morning on a weekday, or around a mealtime. Ask whether you can stay for lunch. If a second visit is possible, go at a different time of day, perhaps late afternoon or a weekend, to see how things change.
Write your questions down
It is easy to forget questions in the moment. Bring a short list, and ask each community the same ones so you can compare the answers fairly.
What does a typical day look like for a resident here?
How is support planned with each resident, and how often is it reviewed?
Which team members would we see regularly, and how long have they worked here?
How are families kept informed?
What can residents bring from home?
What is included in the monthly cost, and what is extra?
How is availability handled if the suite we want is not free?
Notice what is not on the tour

Pay attention to the moments between the planned stops. How do staff speak to residents when they pass in a corridor? Are people chatting in the shared rooms, or are the rooms empty? Is the building comfortable, with good light, fresh air and a sensible temperature? Does it smell clean and look cared for in the corners as well as the lobby?
Look at a suite like the one you are considering, not only the model suite. Sit in a chair in the dining room. Step outside. Imagine an ordinary day.
Talk to the people who live there
If residents are happy to talk, ask them what they enjoy and what they would change. Most people are honest, and their answers are often more useful than any brochure.
Take notes and photographs

After three or four visits, details blur. Take brief notes immediately afterward, and if photography is permitted, take a few pictures of the suite and the shared spaces. Note your overall impression in a sentence: did it feel like a place you would want to visit again?
Plan to come back

A first visit is rarely the last. If a community feels promising, return with your remaining questions, perhaps with a different family member, and spend more time there. A good community will welcome you back as often as you need.

title: Maintaining independence during a move to senior living
summary: Moving into a community can strengthen independence rather than reduce it. Here is how to keep choice and control at the center of the change.

image.alt: An older couple walk together on a lakeside path between birch trees.

children.text: For many older adults, the hardest part of moving to senior living is not the packing. It is the worry that moving means giving something up: privacy, control, a sense of being in charge of one's own life. That worry is understandable, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Handled well, a move can actually protect independence, by removing the chores and isolation that were quietly limiting it.
Make it the resident's decision

The single most important factor is who makes the decision. When an older adult leads the choice, visiting communities, asking the questions and choosing the suite, the move becomes an act of independence rather than a loss of it. Families can help with research and logistics, but the final say should rest with the person who will live there whenever possible.
If a decision has to be made more quickly than anyone would like, keep as many smaller choices as possible in the resident's hands: which suite, which furniture, which day to move, who helps.
Bring routines along

Daily routines are a large part of who we are. Before the move, it can help to write down the habits that matter: the time of the first cup of coffee, a favorite radio program, the daily walk, the crossword, a weekly phone call. Share this with the new community and ask how those routines can continue. A good community will build around them rather than replace them.
Choose help, rather than accepting it

Independence is not doing everything alone; it is deciding what to do yourself and what to hand off. Many residents find that giving up cooking or housekeeping frees time and energy for what they actually enjoy. Others want to keep cooking a favorite dish or tending their own plants. Ask the community how support is planned with each person and how easy it is to change those choices over time.
Keep connections outside

Moving should not mean leaving a life behind. Keep up memberships, friendships, places of worship and volunteering wherever possible. Ask about transportation and whether friends can visit easily. Staying connected to the wider world is one of the strongest supports for independence there is.
Find a role

People thrive when they are useful and recognized. Many communities welcome residents who want to lead a club, teach a skill, welcome new neighbors or help plan events. Ask what is possible, and consider what you would enjoy contributing.
Give it time

Most people need several weeks, sometimes a few months, to feel settled anywhere new. Early tiredness or homesickness is normal. Keep an eye on whether things are improving over time, and talk to the community team about anything that is not working. Adjustments are part of the process.
For families
Supporting independence sometimes means stepping back. Ask before helping, let your relative set the pace and resist the urge to manage every detail. Your role is to be an ally, not a supervisor.

title: Helping a loved one feel comfortable in a new home
summary: Practical ideas for the weeks before and after moving day, so a new suite starts to feel like home sooner.

image.alt: A walnut dresser and a tall mirror reflecting the bed, beside a window onto the woods.

children.text: Moving into a senior living community is a big change, even when it is the right one. The first few weeks set the tone. With some thoughtful preparation, families can help a new suite feel familiar quickly and make the transition gentler for everyone.
Plan the suite together

Ask the community for a floor plan with measurements, and plan the layout with your relative. Choose the pieces that matter most: a favorite chair, a bedside table, a bookcase, the lamp that always sat by the window. Familiar furniture placed in a familiar arrangement can make a new room feel known on the very first night.
It is tempting to bring everything. Resist that. A suite that feels crowded can be harder to live in. Start with what matters most and add over time.
Bring the details that make a place personal
Photographs of family, friends and favorite places.
A familiar bedspread, blanket or cushions.
Books, music and a radio or speaker.
Small objects with meaning: a clock, a vase, a piece of art.
Practical favorites: the coffee mug, the reading glasses, the good scissors.
Set up before arrival, if possible

If the community allows it, arrange furniture, hang pictures and make the bed before your relative arrives. Walking into a room that is already theirs is very different from walking into a room full of boxes. Ask whether the maintenance team can help with hanging pictures or installing shelves.
Share what matters with the team

Tell the community team about your relative's routines, preferences and history: how they like their tea, what time they wake, what they did for a living, what topics bring them to life. The more the team knows, the faster they can make your relative feel known.
Visit, but leave room

Regular visits are reassuring, especially at first. But it also helps to leave space for new friendships and routines to form. Join a meal or an event together, introduce your relative to a neighbor, then let them find their own way. Ask the team for a quiet update after the first week or two.
Expect ups and downs

Settling in takes time. Some days will be harder than others, and that is normal. Listen to concerns, take them seriously and raise them with the community team so they can be addressed. If something is not working, it can usually be adjusted.
Look after yourself, too

Family members often carry a great deal during a move, practically and emotionally. It is fine to feel relief and sadness at the same time. Make time to rest, and lean on others who have been through it.
When you are ready, our team is happy to talk through how Evermere helps new residents settle in.

question: Can I bring family members to a visit?

children.text: Yes. Many visits include a prospective resident and one or more family members, and we encourage everyone involved in the decision to come.

question: What kinds of suites are available?

children.text: Evermere has studio suites, one-bedroom suites and lakeside suites. Each has a private bathroom, a kitchenette and windows onto the courtyard or the lake.
See the accommodations

question: Can I bring my own furniture?

children.text: Yes, and we encourage it. We will help you plan what fits before moving day, and our maintenance team will hang pictures and set up your furniture. If you prefer, a suite can be furnished with simple pieces instead.
Yes. Couples can share a larger suite. If partners need different levels of support, we will talk openly about the options.

question: Is there a set daily schedule?

children.text: There is a calendar of classes, clubs, meals and outings, but residents decide how to spend their own time. Getting up late, skipping a class or spending an afternoon alone is entirely your choice.
Meals are cooked from scratch in our own kitchen, with seasonal Washington ingredients. Breakfast, lunch and dinner are served in the Dining Room, and snacks and drinks are available between meals.
See how we dine

question: Can the kitchen accommodate dietary needs?

children.text: The culinary team accommodates many dietary preferences and needs. Talk with us about specific requirements so we can explain what is possible.
Art, music, gardening, lectures, book clubs, gentle exercise, walks along the shore and regular outings around the Sound. Residents help plan the calendar and are welcome to start new groups.
Discover daily life
Family and friends are welcome at any reasonable hour, and they are welcome to join meals and events. A guest suite can be reserved for relatives traveling from farther away.

question: How will our family be kept informed?

children.text: We agree with each resident how and when their family will be updated, and we follow that agreement. Families can always reach a member of our team with questions.
Pet arrangements depend on the animal and the suite. Please ask, and we will talk through the details with you.

question: What kind of support is available?

children.text: Support is planned with each resident around their routines and preferences, from help with daily tasks to household services and transportation. The specific services available are explained in a personal consultation.
Read about care and support

question: What happens if my needs change?

children.text: Personal plans are reviewed regularly and whenever something changes. We will always talk honestly with you and your family about what Evermere can provide.

question: How much does it cost to live at Evermere?

children.text: Costs depend on the suite and the support each person chooses, so we do not publish a single price. We are glad to explain costs clearly and in writing during a personal conversation.
Talk with our team

question: Is there a suite available now?

children.text: Availability changes throughout the year. Contact us for current availability, and we can let you know when a particular type of suite becomes free.
